candidates.attacker_control: An authenticated HTTP client fully controls the POST body of /rest/v1/appointmentscheduling/createappointment (patient, status, appointmentType, visit, date, location, provider UUIDs). The appointment date, location and provider directly parameterize createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule, and thus the start/end time, provider, location and types of the AppointmentBlock and TimeSlot that are persisted.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Bare @Authorized is an OpenMRS idiom meaning 'authenticated user only' (the method deliberately has no privilege value), so this may be an intentional-but-weak design for the requisition flow rather than an injected defect; I could not execute the OpenMRS AuthorizedInterceptor to confirm semantics, and the P1 index contains no proof of runtime behavior. However, the module explicitly defines 'Manage Provider Schedules' as the ability to add/edit/purge appointment blocks, the equivalent save methods are annotated with it, and the write reaches the database through DAOs with no check anywhere on the path; the controller performs no Context.hasPrivilege check either. I also considered that the REST route may be reachable only through the webservices.rest module's dispatcher, which I could not verify by execution.
candidates.impact: Unauthorized integrity modification of scheduling data: an authenticated user without the 'Manage Provider Schedules' privilege can create arbitrary AppointmentBlock and TimeSlot records (and thus bogus availability) for any provider/location where a provider schedule exists, repeatedly, enabling scheduling-data pollution and resource exhaustion. Where a matching appointment type/visit is also provided, the same flow can contribute to unauthorized bookings if the user also holds Schedule Appointments.
candidates.prerequisites: Authenticated session (the endpoint requires authentication but no appointment privilege); the caller needs core view privileges for the referenced patient/visit/appointment type; a ProviderSchedule must already exist for the chosen location/provider/time; the provider/location must match the schedule; the endpoint must be routed by the webservices.rest dispatcher to this module controller (not runtime-verified here).
candidates.root_cause: In the service interface, state-changing methods that create scheduling records carry @Authorized(AppointmentUtils.PRIV_MANAGE_APPOINTMENT_BLOCKS) (e.g. saveAppointmentBlock, saveTimeSlot), but createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule only carries a bare @Authorized (OpenMRS semantics: any authenticated user, no privilege). The implementation then writes directly through the DAOs (getAppointmentBlockDAO().saveOrUpdate(...), getTimeSlotDAO().saveOrUpdate(...)), so no service-layer privilege interceptor runs for the write. A custom REST controller exposes this path with attacker-supplied parameters and no privilege gate.
candidates.title: Missing privilege on createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule allows any authenticated user to create appointment blocks/time slots via POST /rest/v1/appointmentscheduling/createappointment
candidates.trace: AppointmentRequisitionController.createAppointment (POST mapping lines 27-34) resolves the request body, calls service.getTimeslotForAppointment(...) at lines 44-45, and if no slot exists calls service.createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule(appointmentDate, provider, location) at lines 47-48. That interface method (AppointmentService.java line 1116) is annotated only @Authorized (authentication), unlike saveAppointmentBlock/saveTimeSlot (lines 214, 416, PRIV_MANAGE_APPOINTMENT_BLOCKS). The implementation (AppointmentServiceImpl.java lines 1276-1298) loads ProviderSchedule rows directly through the DAO, builds an AppointmentBlock, persists it via getAppointmentBlockDAO().saveOrUpdate (line 1292) and persists a TimeSlot via getTimeSlotDAO().saveOrUpdate (line 1298); the interceptor cannot add a privilege requirement for these DAO writes. The subsequent bookAppointment call (line 55) does require PRIV_SCHEDULE_APPOINTMENTS, but by then the block/time slot rows have already been written (the controller is not transactional), so the unauthorized write succeeds even when booking is rejected.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: OpenMRS bare-@Authorized semantics, actual servlet routing of the /rest/v1/... controller, and whether any deployment-level filter adds a privilege gate are unverified. No call was executed and no target contacted.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-862/CWE-863 Missing or Incorrect Authorization on a state-changing API

coverage_summary: Same 191-file snapshot and filters for B0/P1 (no binaries or symlinks excluded; no files over 5 MiB). get_relation_scope reports index_status complete for all 191 files with 0 hash mismatches, but only syntactic navigation candidates (calls/containment/inheritance/route/input facts; its 'injection' facts are Spring DI annotations, not SQLi findings). I read essentially all first-party Java under api/src/main/java and omod/src/main/java (service interface and impl, Hibernate DAOs, validators, reporting evaluators/definitions, DWR service, all REST resources and controllers, editors, extensions), plus config.xml, moduleApplicationContext.xml, webModuleApplicationContext.xml, hibernate mappings, liquibase.xml, poms and the workflow. Third-party minified JS/CSS, messages.properties content and hbm.xml mapping details were only spot-checked; no tests exist in the snapshot and no build/scan/runtime verification was performed.
limitations: No code executed, no build, no scanner, no runtime or HTTP request: reachability of /rest/v1/appointmentscheduling/createappointment through the webservices.rest dispatcher and OpenMRS bare-@Authorized interceptor semantics are reasoned from source/convention, not confirmed.
The P1 relation index is syntactic only (no data-flow, reachability or exploitability proof); its facts were used for navigation and every cited edge was verified in source text.
Absence of Spring/JDK/OpenMRS framework sources in the snapshot means the exact behavior of Context.hasPrivilege, AuthorizedInterceptor and REST authentication filters could not be inspected locally.
No test files exist in the snapshot, so no test names or fixtures were available to corroborate intended privilege behavior.

Third-party JavaScript/CSS (jQuery, fullcalendar, jqPlot, ZeroClipboard, TableTools) and message bundles were not exhaustively reviewed for client-side issues; they are out of the traced server-side attack path.

Alternative authorization/confidentiality leads (overbooking, confidential filtering, status-change privilege, misspelled privileges) remain unconfirmed and were not submitted as additional candidates per the one-candidate cap.

rejected_leads.lead: Overbooking privilege bypass: bookAppointment is annotated only with PRIV_SCHEDULE_APPOINTMENTS while AppointmentAllowingOverbookResource1_9.save passes allowOverbook=true and skips the capacity check in AppointmentServiceImpl (lines 1185-1190); the 'Squeezing Appointments' privilege is enforced only client-side in AppointmentFormController (line 135).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible authorization weakness (CWE-863), but the API design intentionally parameterizes the bypass (allowOverbook) for the UI flow and the concrete impact is a scheduling-capacity/business-rule violation rather than a high-severity security impact, so it was kept as a secondary lead rather than the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Confidential appointment details exposed without the 'Task: appointmentschedulingui.viewConfidential' privilege: only PatientToAppointmentDataEvaluator (line 47) and PersonToAppointmentDataEvaluator (line 50) filter confidential appointments; AppointmentPropertyDataEvaluator (reason/creator/etc.) and the REST/legacy read paths (AppointmentResource1_9, AppointmentListController, AppointmentsPortletController) return details to users with only View Appointments.
rejected_leads.reason: Real confidentiality concern, but the privilege is named for the appointmentschedulingui UI module and is never consulted in this module's REST/web read code, so the intended scope of protection is inferable rather than demonstrable from the source; confidence that it is the strongest evidence-supported issue is lower than for the missing write authorization.

rejected_leads.lead: PRIV_UPDATE_APPOINTMENT_STATES defined/used in the UI only (PatientDashboardAppointmentExt line 32), while changeAppointmentStatus uses PRIV_SCHEDULE_APPOINTMENTS (AppointmentService line 869), letting Schedule Appointments users cancel/complete/miss appointments.
rejected_leads.reason: Same class of client-side-only privilege enforcement as the overbooking lead; ambiguous whether scheduling privilege is meant to subsume status changes, and lower confidentiality/integrity delta.

rejected_leads.lead: voidAppointment/voidTimeSlot/voidAppointmentRequest do not set voided/voidReason (AppointmentServiceImpl lines 406-414, 470-478, 604-614), so REST DELETE may not actually void records.
rejected_leads.reason: Functional correctness bug visible in source, not an attacker-controlled security boundary violation; impact is data-state semantics, not unauthorized access.

rejected_leads.lead: Privilege constants PRIV_VIEW_PROVIDER_SCHEDULES / PRIV_MANAGE_PROVIDER_SCHEDULES are misspelled ('Scedules') versus config.xml 'View Provider Schedules'/'Manage Provider Schedules'.
rejected_leads.reason: Fail-closed: Context.hasPrivilege on a nonexistent privilege name denies access (possible functional breakage), not a privilege escalation.

rejected_leads.lead: Vendored jQuery 1.9.1/jQuery UI/fullcalendar/jqPlot/ZeroClipboard versions under omod webapp resources.
rejected_leads.reason: Third-party libraries; no concrete first-party exploit path or usage evidence in the reviewed Java code, and version-comparison would require external data not available in this run.

summary: Reviewed the OpenMRS appointment scheduling module snapshot (1.17.0-SNAPSHOT) at source level: 191 files under the same read-only filters for B0/P1; the P1 relation index covers all 191 files but is syntactic only (its "injection" facts are Spring @Autowired noise, not SAST findings). I traced the web/REST/DWR entry points, service-layer @Authorized annotations, Hibernate DAO queries, validators, reporting evaluators and configurations. DAO queries are parameterized/Criteria-based; no SQL/HQL injection, deserialization, file/path, command-execution, or hardcoded-secret sink was found. The strongest source-supported issue is missing authorization on a state-changing service operation that is reachable from a network endpoint: createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule is annotated with a bare @Authorized (authentication only) although it persists AppointmentBlock and TimeSlot rows via DAOs, while every comparable write method requires "Manage Provider Schedules". Its caller, AppointmentRequisitionController, is a POST REST endpoint that passes attacker-controlled provider/location/date values with no privilege check, so any authenticated user with basic view privileges can create scheduling records without Manage Provider Schedules.
